lessons.title: Modules, pip and virtual environments
lessons.objective: By the end you can import from the standard library and from your own files, create a virtual environment, install a package with pip, and record your dependencies in requirements.txt.
concept: A **module** is just a `.py` file you can import. `import math` loads a standard-library module, and you use its contents with a dot, as in `math.sqrt(16)`. `from random import randint` imports a single name directly. Python ships with a huge **standard library** (`random`, `math`, `datetime`, `json`, `csv`, `pathlib`, `statistics` and many more), so check it before you write something yourself. Your own files work the same way: if `helpers.py` sits next to `main.py`, then `import helpers` in main gives you `helpers.some_function()`.

When Python imports a file, it **runs** the whole thing. So a file that's both a module and a script puts its "run me" code under `if __name__ == "__main__":`. That block runs when you execute the file directly, but not when another file imports it, which makes it the natural place to call `main()`. Never name your own file after a module you use, such as `random.py` or `json.py`. Your file gets imported instead, and you'll see baffling errors.

Packages outside the standard library live on PyPI and are installed with **pip**. Install them into a **virtual environment**, a private folder of packages for each project, so projects don't fight over versions. Run `python3 -m venv .venv`, then `source .venv/bin/activate` (`.venv\Scripts\activate` on Windows), then `pip install requests`. Record what the project needs with `pip freeze > requirements.txt`, and anyone can recreate the setup with `pip install -r requirements.txt`. Add `.venv/` to `.gitignore`. Commit the requirements file, not the folder.

steps.label: Create
steps.detail: python3 -m venv .venv

steps.label: Activate
steps.detail: source .venv/bin/activate (the prompt shows (.venv))

steps.label: Install
steps.detail: pip install requests

steps.label: Record
steps.detail: pip freeze > requirements.txt

example.code:
import math
import random
from datetime import date
from statistics import mean

roll = random.randint(1, 6)
print("You rolled", roll)
print(math.sqrt(81), math.ceil(4.1), round(mean([2, 3, 7]), 2))
print(date(2026, 1, 1).strftime("%A"))

def main():
    print("running as a script")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
example.explain: Four standard-library modules, imported in two styles. With `import math` you write `math.` before each name, while `from statistics import mean` lets you call mean directly. strftime("%A") gives the weekday name: 1 January 2026 is a Thursday. main() runs only because this file was executed directly rather than imported.

lessons.tryit: In a new folder, create and activate a virtual environment, run `pip install requests`, and write a 5-line script that fetches https://api.github.com and prints `response.status_code`. Freeze your requirements, add `.venv/` to `.gitignore`, and commit. Then split an earlier project into `logic.py` (pure functions) and `main.py` (input and printing), joined by `import logic`.

options: It makes the file run faster
It runs its block only when the file is executed directly, not when it's imported
It's required at the top of every Python file
questions.explain: When you run a file, Python sets its __name__ to "__main__". When the file is imported, __name__ is the module's name instead. This guard lets one file work as both a reusable module and a runnable script.

questions.code:
import math
print(math.floor(7.8), math.sqrt(49))
questions.explain: floor rounds down to the int 7. sqrt always returns a float, even for a perfect square, so you get 7.0.

questions.code:
from datetime import date
print((date(2026, 3, 1) - date(2026, 2, 1)).days)
questions.explain: Subtracting two dates gives a timedelta, and its .days attribute is the gap in days. February 2026 has 28 days, because 2026 isn't a leap year.

questions.prompt: You saved a script as `random.py` containing `import random` and `print(random.randint(1, 6))`. Running it fails with an AttributeError about randint. Why?
options: Your file is named random.py, so `import random` imports your own file instead of the standard library
randint only works inside a virtual environment
questions.explain: Python searches the script's own folder before the standard library, so your file shadows the real module, and it has no randint. Rename the file, for example to dice.py, and delete any `__pycache__` folder that was created. random is in the standard library, so there's nothing to pip install.

project.title: CSV data cleaner
project.brief: Build `clean.py`, a command-line tool that takes a messy CSV export (inconsistent capitalisation, stray spaces, blank rows, bad numbers, duplicate rows) and writes a clean CSV plus a JSON report of what it fixed. Real data is always messy, so this is one of the most reusable programs you'll ever write, and it uses files, csv, json, exceptions and modules together. For practice data, download any public CSV (data.gov has thousands) or hand-make a 30-row file with deliberate mistakes.

Drop duplicates (a set of tuples works well as a record of rows you've seen), write `clean.csv` with csv.DictWriter, and write `report.json` with counts of rows read, fixed, rejected and duplicated.

exam.explain: "3" converts and gives 12 // 3 = 4. "x" fails inside int(), which is a ValueError. "0" converts fine but 12 // 0 is a ZeroDivisionError. Each except clause catches only its own type, and the try sits inside the loop, so processing continues after each failure.

exam.prompt: This is meant to load the contacts. It crashes, and afterwards contacts.json is empty. Why?

import json
with open("contacts.json", "w") as f:
    contacts = json.load(f)

The file must be closed before json.load

print(back["scores"], back == data)

    for i in range(3):
        f.write(f"line {i}\n")

    f.write("end\n")

exam.prompt: A cleaner should skip bad rows and keep processing the rest. Where should the try/except go?
options: Inside the loop body, around the conversion of each row
In a finally block after the loop
exam.explain: With the try inside the loop, an error affects only the current row, and the loop moves on to the next one. With the try around the whole loop, the first bad row jumps out of the loop and every row after it is skipped.

exam.prompt: A teammate clones your repo, which contains requirements.txt but not .venv/. What should they run to get the same packages?

Copy your .venv folder from your laptop

modules.title: Objects and recursion
modules.summary: Model things as objects that protect their own rules, solve self-similar problems recursively, and plan a 300-line program from scratch.

lessons.title: Classes and methods
lessons.objective: By the end you can define a class with __init__ and methods, create several independent instances, and explain what self refers to.
concept: A **class** is a blueprint for a kind of object. It bundles **data** (attributes) with the **functions that work on that data** (methods). `class BankAccount:` describes what every account has and can do, and `acct = BankAccount("Ana", 100)` creates one **instance** of it. You can make as many instances as you like, and each keeps its own data, so depositing into Ana's account doesn't touch Ben's.

`__init__` is the method Python calls automatically when you create an instance. It sets up the starting attributes, as in `self.owner = owner`. **`self`** is the instance the method is working on. When you write `acct.deposit(50)`, Python calls `BankAccount.deposit(acct, 50)`, so the object before the dot becomes `self`. That's why every method's first parameter is `self`, and why attributes are always written `self.something` inside methods. In the trace, watch `self` inside `add` show the same object as `c`.

Methods can read and change attributes, return values and call other methods. A `__str__` method returns the text `print(acct)` should show. Without one, you get something like `<__main__.BankAccount object at 0x10f3...>`. Class names use `CapitalizedWords`, and method and attribute names use `snake_case`. You've been using objects all along: `"hi".upper()` calls the `upper` method on a `str` instance, and `nums.append(4)` calls a method on a list instance.

lessons.title: When to use a class
lessons.objective: By the end you can decide whether plain data plus functions or a class is the better design for a problem, and design a class that protects its own rules.
concept: Classes aren't automatically better. A dict and a few functions, such as `account = {"owner": "Ana", "balance": 100}` with `deposit(account, 50)`, are often perfectly fine, especially for simple records you load from JSON. Reach for a class when **data and behaviour belong together**, so that you'd otherwise pass the same dict to the same handful of functions everywhere, or when you have several *kinds* of a thing to keep straight.

The strongest reason for a class is **invariants**: rules that must always be true. "The balance never goes negative." "A category's spent amount always equals the sum of its transactions." If every change goes through methods (`withdraw` checks the balance first), the rule is enforced in one place. With a bare dict, any line anywhere can run `account["balance"] = -500`, and you'll have to hunt for it.

There are warning signs of an unnecessary class. If it has only `__init__` and one other method, it's really a function. If it has no methods at all, it's really a dict, or a `@dataclass`, a shortcut for data-only classes you'll meet soon. Signs that you do need one: several functions all take the same first argument, or a comment says "don't change X without also updating Y". For the capstone, a sensible split is classes for the core things (`Transaction`, `Budget`) and plain functions for loading, saving and the menu.

lessons.title: Recursion and the call stack
lessons.objective: By the end you can write a recursive function with a base case and a recursive case, and trace its calls on the call stack.
concept: A **recursive** function is one that calls itself on a smaller version of the same problem. Factorial is the classic example: 4! = 4 × 3!, 3! = 3 × 2!, and so on, down to 1! = 1. Every recursive function needs two parts: a **base case** that answers the smallest problem directly, without recursing (`if n == 1: return 1`), and a **recursive case** that makes the problem smaller and calls itself (`return n * fact(n - 1)`).

Each call gets its own **stack frame**, its own private set of local variables, stacked on top of its caller's. When `fact(3)` calls `fact(2)`, the `fact(3)` frame pauses and waits, with its own `n = 3` still intact. When the base case returns, the frames **unwind** one by one, each finishing its multiplication with the value it got back. Step through the trace and watch three different `n`s exist at once, then disappear in reverse order as each call returns its value.

If the base case is missing or never reached (say, `fact(0)` with a base case of `n == 1`, or a call that forgets to subtract), the calls go on until Python's safety limit of about 1,000 frames and you get `RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded`. When you write a recursive function, ask yourself three questions. What's the smallest input, and what's its answer? How does each call make the problem smaller? Does every path eventually reach the base case?

visual.title: fact(3) on the call stack

example.explain: `countdown` shrinks n by 1 on each call, and its base case is 0. `total` shrinks the list by slicing off the first item, and its base case is the empty list, whose total is 0. So total([4, 5, 6]) is 4 + total([5, 6]), which is 4 + 5 + total([6]), and so on, giving 15.

lessons.tryit: Write `power(base, exp)` recursively, with the base case exp == 0 returning 1. Before running `power(2, 3)`, draw the stack of calls on paper, showing each frame's variables and the value it returns. Then write `count_char(text, ch)` recursively (look at `text[0]`, and recurse on `text[1:]`) and test both functions with asserts, including the empty string.

questions.prompt: Which part of a recursive function stops the recursion?
questions.explain: The base case answers the smallest problem directly, without another call. Without it, or if it's never reached, you get a RecursionError.

mystery(7) is 7 + mystery(5), which is 7 + 5 + mystery(3), then 7 + 5 + 3 + mystery(1), then 7 + 5 + 3 + 1 + mystery(-1). mystery(-1) hits the base case and returns 0, so the answer is 16. Note that the base case uses <= 0, so odd numbers still stop.

The print comes *after* the recursive call, so each frame waits for all the deeper calls to finish before printing. show(1) is the first to get past its call, so it prints first, and the output runs in increasing order as the stack unwinds. Put the print before the call and you'd get 3 2 1.

n goes 0, -1, -2, ... and never equals 1, so the base case is never reached, and Python stops the program after about 1,000 frames. A safer base case is `if n <= 1: return 1`, which also gives the correct answer of 1 for 0!.

lessons.title: Recursion vs iteration
lessons.objective: By the end you can rewrite a simple recursive function as a loop and vice versa, decide which approach fits a problem, and spot recursion that repeats work exponentially.
concept: Anything a loop can do, recursion can do, and the other way round. For straight-line problems, such as summing a list, counting down or computing a factorial, a loop is usually clearer and faster in Python, and it can't hit the recursion limit. `sum_to(100_000)` written recursively crashes, while the loop version finishes instantly. Python doesn't optimise deep recursion, so for "do this n times" problems, prefer iteration.

Recursion wins when the data itself is recursive. A folder contains files *and folders*. A comment thread contains replies, which contain replies. A menu contains submenus. "Process this folder" naturally means "process each file, and for each subfolder, process that folder", which is a recursive call. Writing that with loops means managing your own list of things still to visit. Branching searches, such as trying every combination or solving a maze, are the same story.

Watch out for recursion that repeats work. The textbook `fib(n) = fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)` looks elegant, but `fib(n - 1)` recomputes everything `fib(n - 2)` has already done, so the number of calls roughly doubles with each step. `fib(35)` makes about 30 million calls. A simple loop that keeps the last two values does it in 35 steps. The fix for recursive versions is to remember answers you've already computed (memoisation), which you'll meet properly in Stage 2.

left.title: Loop (iteration)
points: State lives in variables you update (total, i)
Best for counting, summing and walking a flat list
No depth limit, and usually faster in Python
Fibonacci with a loop: n steps

right.title: Recursion
points: State lives in each call's parameters
Best for nested data: folders, menus, JSON, mazes
Limited to about 1,000 nested calls by default
Naive recursive Fibonacci: exponentially many calls (fixed by memoising)

example.explain: `nested_sum` mixes both approaches: a loop walks across one level, and recursion goes down into each sub-list. That's the natural shape for nested data. `fib_loop` keeps just the last two values, so even fib_loop(50) takes 50 cheap steps. The naive recursive version would make tens of billions of calls.

Then write a recursive `count_files(tree)`, where a tree is a dict like `{"docs": {"a.txt": None, "old": {"b.txt": None}}, "c.txt": None}` (None means a file and a dict means a folder), and check that it returns 3.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many nested calls does Python allow by default before raising RecursionError?
questions.explain: The default recursion limit is 1000 (see sys.getrecursionlimit()). It protects the program from crashing outright. You can raise it, but deep recursion is usually a sign that a loop would be better.

questions.prompt: How many times is fib called in total? What does this print?
questions.explain: Count the calls tree-style: calls(n) = 1 + calls(n - 1) + calls(n - 2), with calls(0) = calls(1) = 1. That gives 1, 1, 3, 5, 9, 15 for n = 0 to 5. Just computing fib(5) = 5 takes 15 calls, and the count keeps growing exponentially.

questions.prompt: Which task is the most natural fit for recursion?
options: Adding up 1 million numbers in a list
Printing every file in a folder and all its subfolders, however deep
Counting how many times "e" appears in a sentence
Asking for input until the user types quit
questions.explain: Folders contain folders to any depth, so "process a folder" naturally calls itself on each subfolder. The other tasks are flat. A loop handles them more simply, and a million-deep recursion would hit the limit.

questions.prompt: Which loop prints the same thing as `countdown(n)`?
questions.explain: countdown prints n, n - 1, ..., 1, then stops at 0. range(n, 0, -1) produces exactly those values. Option 1 counts up from 0, option 3 is empty (without a negative step it can't count down), and option 4 never changes n, so it loops forever.

lessons.title: Capstone planning: designing a 300-line program
lessons.objective: By the end you can produce a one-page design for a 300-line program, covering features, data model, file layout, function list and build order, before writing the code.
concept: A 300-line program fails differently from a 30-line one. No single line is hard, but you lose track of the whole. The cure is a short design written **before** you code. Put it in `PLAN.md`: (1) what the program does, in three sentences; (2) the **must-have** features as a numbered list, plus a separate *nice-to-have* list; (3) the **data model**, meaning exactly what you store and its shape, for example `{"categories": {"Food": 300}, "transactions": [{"date": "2026-10-20", "amount": 12.5, "category": "Food", "note": "lunch"}]}`.

Next comes the **structure**. Keep the core logic separate from input and output, just as you did in Module 3. `budget.py` holds classes or pure functions, such as adding a transaction or totalling each category, all testable with asserts. `storage.py` loads and saves the JSON, and handles a missing or corrupt file. `main.py` holds the menu loop, `input()` and printing. List every function with its parameters and return value. If you can't describe a function in one sentence, split it.

Then plan the **build order** as vertical slices, each one runnable. First, "add a transaction and list them", end to end, with no saving. Then saving and loading, then category totals, then validation and error messages, then the extras. Commit to Git after every slice that works, so you can always go back. Expect the plan to change, and when it does, update `PLAN.md` rather than keeping the change in your head. A plan you've revised five times is a plan that's doing its job.

options: One file of the program, finished completely before starting the next
A thin feature that works end to end, from the menu through the logic to the output, and that you can run and commit
The top half of the source code
A list of all the functions in the program

questions.prompt: Which file layout makes the budget logic easiest to test?
options: One main.py where each menu option's code computes totals and prints them inline
budget.py with pure functions or classes (no input or print), storage.py for JSON, and main.py for the menu
A separate file for every function
All logic inside the save() function so data is always saved

questions.prompt: You're 150 lines in and realise every transaction needs a date, which you didn't plan for. Existing users already have saved files without dates. What's the best move?

Update PLAN.md and the data model, add the field to new transactions, and have load() give old transactions a default date
Store the dates in a separate file so the existing code doesn't change
Ignore dates until the end of the project
questions.explain: Plans change, and that's normal. Record the change, then handle the old data in one place (load), so the rest of the code can assume every transaction has a date. A separate dates file creates two sources of truth that will drift apart, and starting over throws away 150 working lines.

project.title: Capstone: terminal budgeting app
project.brief: Build a terminal budgeting app of about 300 lines, starting from an empty folder. You set monthly category limits, record income and expenses, see what's left in each category, and keep everything between runs in a JSON file. It's the whole stage in one program: classes for the core model, functions and tests for the logic, collections for the data, files and exceptions for persistence, and a plan you write first. If budgeting doesn't interest you, any program of similar size with saved data (a habit tracker, reading log or flashcards) is fine, as long as you keep the same milestones.
milestones: Write PLAN.md (description, must-haves, JSON data shape, files and function signatures, build slices) and commit it before writing any code.

Build the core model in `budget.py`, either as `Budget` and `Transaction` classes or as pure functions on a dict, with a `test_` function of asserts covering adding transactions, totals per category and detecting a category that's over its limit.
Add `storage.py` with JSON load and save. A missing file should start a fresh budget, and a corrupt file should be backed up and reported rather than crashing the app.

Write the menu in `main.py`: add an expense or income, list one month's transactions, show a category report with the amount remaining, edit category limits, and quit. Validate every number the user types through a single `ask_float()` helper.
Add a report that flags categories over 80% of their limit, and a CSV export of the month's transactions.
Polish: docstrings on every function, `if __name__ == "__main__":`, a README explaining how to run it, and a read-through to split any function over about 25 lines. Check the size with `wc -l *.py`.
project.stretch: Add recurring transactions (such as rent on the 1st of every month) that are created automatically when the app starts in a new month, plus a recursive function that prints category groups nested to any depth (Food → Groceries → Fruit).

Each call strips the last digit with // 10: 40213, 4021, 402, 40, 4. The last call hits the base case (4 < 10). That's 1 from the base case plus 1 for each of the four calls before it, which makes 5.

Each call puts the first character *after* the reversed rest: rev("stack") is rev("tack") + "s", which is rev("ack") + "t" + "s", and so on down to the empty string. The result is "kcats".

exam.prompt: `json.dump(budget, f)`, where budget is an instance of your Budget class, raises `TypeError: Object of type Budget is not JSON serializable`. What's the best fix?

The loop walks across each level, and recursion goes down into each sub-list. Each recursive call returns a flat list, which `out +=` extends onto the current one, so the order of the original items is kept.

Each item adds a stack frame, which exceeds the recursion limit of about 1,000. Use a loop or sum(nums)
